abstract: |
  When several variables are observed over the same hierarchy, it seems natural to reconcile their forecasts jointly so that cross-variable dependence can inform the adjustment. We investigate when joint reconciliation improves on reconciling each variable separately. Writing minimum trace reconciliation as a regression of the base forecast errors on the observed incoherences, we show that joint and separate reconciliation coincide if and only if each variable's separately reconciled errors are uncorrelated with the other variables' incoherences. Separable error covariances, dependence confined to the coherent part of the errors, and simulation designs in which every node shares the same dynamics are all special cases. We propose two effect sizes and a likelihood ratio test of this condition. In simulations, joint reconciliation reduces the mean squared error by at most `r targets::tar_read(numbers)$gainFtwoBrazilMax`% even when the error covariance is known, and with an estimated covariance it is less accurate than separate reconciliation at small sample sizes because it must estimate the cross-variable covariances. For monthly Brazilian employment data over 2007--2019, the test detects a small departure from the condition, but with ARIMA base forecasts joint reconciliation does not systematically improve the forecasts of either admissions or dismissals. It does reduce the mean squared error of national net employment change by `r targets::tar_read(numbers)$appNetPointTotal`%, and for probabilistic forecasts of net change most of the gain comes from simulating the base forecasts jointly, which reduces the CRPS by `r targets::tar_read(numbers)$appNetJointSepTotal`%. Separate reconciliation is usually sufficient for forecasting each variable, but the dependence between variables should be modelled when the quantity of interest combines them.
